paras: The rumored Ferguson raid on Lix Park was a June 1919 scare in Kinloch, St. Louis County, Missouri, when residents expected people from neighboring Ferguson to raid the Lix Park outing place at night. Many Kinloch women and children left for the night, but no mob came. The St. Louis Argus reported the episode to correct what it called an exaggerated account in a St. Louis daily.

Lix Park was an outing place at Kinloch reached by streetcar, offering music, dancing and barbecue. Car conductors told the Argus that picnickers caused little trouble and Kinloch residents none, and that disputes on the line were generally over car fare.

The trouble began in mid-June, when a conductor on the Kirkwood-Ferguson line slapped a Colored woman during an argument about car fare. Some Colored men afterward beat the conductor. The beating, the Argus wrote, seemed to arouse the indignation of Ferguson residents, and word spread in Kinloch that a number of them would make a night raid on Lix Park. Many women and children went away for the night while the men stayed to protect the property, but "the mob movement did not develop."

Kinloch residents then met and petitioned the county prosecuting attorney to bar intoxicating liquor at the park; 155 Colored and 11 white residents signed. One signer said the petition came not from fear of the whites but from a wish to protect Kinloch from "unscrupulous persons" drawn from St. Louis to the resort.

Prosecuting Attorney Ralph said he had taken no action beyond asking some parties to talk with him, while a sheriff's deputy said the proprietors had been ordered to stop selling intoxicating liquor. The park announced that county authorities had let it stay open within the law, serving soft drinks only.

The episode is known from a single front-page story in the St. Louis Argus of June 27, 1919, headed "Car Conductor Starts Trouble for Kinloch Pk.", which placed the blame on the conductor. The Argus wrote that a St. Louis daily had published "an exaggerated and incorrect account" that gave the trouble "unjust seriousness," though some of its statements were later corrected. On the same page, the park's notice answered "one of the afternoon papers" by announcing that Lix Park was still open.

reader.title: Rumored Ferguson raid on Lix Park, Kinloch
bases: The only report describes a rumored night raid by Ferguson residents on a Kinloch park that led women and children to leave, but 'the mob movement did not develop' (A3).

Only the St. Louis Argus report (A3) describes the episode; the park's notice in the same issue (A4) confirms only the surrounding controversy, and the St. Louis daily account it mentions was not found.

accounts.label: St. Louis Argus reporter
accounts.gist: A conductor's slap of a Colored woman and his beating by Colored men stirred Ferguson residents; a rumored night raid on Lix Park sent Kinloch women and children away, but no mob came.

accounts.label: Lix Park management
accounts.gist: An afternoon paper's article had no effect; the park stays open with county approval, serving soft drinks only.

framing.detail: The Argus headline 'Car Conductor Starts Trouble for Kinloch Pk.' put the cause on the conductor, rejected a St. Louis daily's 'exaggerated and incorrect account', and reported conductors' statements that picnickers and Kinloch residents cause little trouble.
The park's own notice in the Argus answered 'one of the afternoon papers' by announcing it was still open.

versions.value: The Argus says a St. Louis daily published an exaggerated and incorrect account that gave the trouble 'unjust seriousness', partly corrected in later issues; that daily's account was not found.

conflicts.note: Only the Argus side of the dispute is available; the St. Louis daily's version could not be compared.

record_check.dossier: No victim is named for the Kinloch episode; Forrest B. Anderson signed an unrelated Kansas City Sun letter about a different streetcar confrontation (A1, A2). The target was Lix Park and the Kinloch community.
Black: the slapped woman is 'Colored' and the rumored raid was on Kinloch, whose petitioners were mostly Colored.
Rumored: a number of Ferguson residents; no raid took place.
A rumored night raid that did not develop, preceded by a conductor slapping a Colored woman and Colored men beating the conductor.
One Black paper (St. Louis Argus, 1919-06-27, two items); the Kansas City Sun item of 1919-06-21 is a different incident.

record_check.record: Rumors said Ferguson residents would make a night raid on Lix Park at Kinloch after a streetcar altercation...
record_check.dossier: Accurate; add that the conductor slapped a Colored woman and was beaten by Colored men, and that the petition was signed by 155 Colored and 11 white residents.

info: The trouble started 'last week' before the Argus of June 27, 1919, i.e. about the third week of June 1919; the prosecutor spoke to the Argus on a Tuesday afterward.
Lix Park, an outing place at Kinloch, a suburb of St. Louis; the conductor worked on the Kirkwood-Ferguson car line; the rumored raiders were residents of Ferguson, 'another suburb'.
No individual victim named; the rumored raid was aimed at Lix Park, and the women and children of Kinloch left for the night. Separately, an unnamed Colored woman was slapped by a car conductor.
None stated against the community; the trigger was the beating of a car conductor by some Colored men after he slapped a Colored woman in a fare dispute.
Rumored: 'a number of' residents of Ferguson, whose indignation was aroused by the beating of the conductor.

sources.note: 'Car Conductor Starts Trouble for Kinloch Pk.': conductor slapped a Colored woman, was beaten; rumored Ferguson night raid on Lix Park did not develop; liquor petition; St. Louis daily's account called exaggerated.
quotes: a conductor on the Kickwood-Ferguson line slapped a Colored woman during an altercation about car fare. The conductor was afterward beaten by some Colored men.
it was rumored in Kinkloo that a number of them were going to make a night raid on Lix Park.
many of the women and children of Kinkloo went away for the night, leaving the men to protect the property, but the mob movement did not develop.
A St. Louis daily newspaper published an exaggerated and incorrect account of the trouble which tended to give it unjust seriousness.

sources.note: 'Lix Park Still Open' notice: an afternoon paper's article had no effect; county authorities allow the park to stay open; soft drinks only.
quotes: An article appearing in one of the afternoon papers, recently, has had no effect upon the operation of Lix Park

set_aside: Opening of a letter to the editor (run with a Detroit hospital item) describing a streetcar confrontation at 24th Street; no mention of Kinloch, Ferguson or Lix Park.
Continuation of the same letter, signed Forrest B. Anderson: a motorman with a switchbar chased two Colored women and about six white men took his side; a separate streetcar incident, not Kinloch.
